procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 3, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench in Criminal Revision Applications No. 410 and 413 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Tribeni, Lalta and Ram Bharosey filed Revision Applications (No. 410 and 413 of 1964) before the Allahabad High Court. The High Court affirmed the order of the Sessions Judge, Gonda and dismissed the Revision Applications on June 3, 1966.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (Tribeni, Lalta, and Ram Bharosey) approached the Supreme Court by special leave after the Allahabad High Court dismissed their Criminal Revision Applications.

directions: The judgment of the Allahabad High Court dated June 3, 1966 must be set aside.
If the appellants are still in jail they should be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rule of issue-estoppel is applicable in criminal trials in India, distinct from the principle of autrefois acquit under Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

facts: The case presented the question of whether the common law principle of 'issue-estoppel' applies in Indian criminal law.
This was considered in light of Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, which codifies the rule against double jeopardy (*autrefois acquit*).
An argument was made that Section 403 was an exhaustive statutory provision, and therefore, there was no room for the separate principle of issue-estoppel.

law.description: A rule preventing a party (in this case, the prosecution) from re-litigating an issue of fact that has already been tried and decided in favor of an accused by a competent court in a previous trial. It acts as a rule of evidence, precluding evidence to disturb the earlier finding, even if the subsequent trial is for a different offence.
A statutory rule that a person who has been tried and acquitted for an offence cannot be tried again for the same offence. This is a plea that bars the entire trial.

application.description: The Court first distinguished between the two principles. It clarified that *autrefois acquit* under Section 403 bars a second trial for the same offence, whereas issue-estoppel bars the re-litigation of a specific issue of fact that was decided in a prior case, even if the second trial is for a different offence.

The Court rejected the argument that Section 403 was exhaustive and excluded the rule of issue-estoppel. It held that while Section 403 does not explicitly cover issue-estoppel, it does not preclude its applicability. The two principles can and do operate distinctly.
The Court affirmed the validity of issue-estoppel in India, stating that the rule is in accordance with 'sound principle' and is supported by 'high authority'.

The Court relied on its own precedents, specifically citing *Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab* and *Manipur Administration v. Thokchom, Bira Singh*, where the rule had already been accepted and applied. In *Pritam Singh*, an acquittal on an arms charge prevented the prosecution from later proving the accused's possession of the same weapon in a murder trial.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the rule of issue-estoppel is applicable in criminal trials in India. It is a principle distinct from, and not precluded by, the statutory rule of *autrefois acquit* contained in Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. The Court found the rule to be sound in principle and affirmed its own previous decisions that had already adopted it.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is exhaustive in character and thereby precludes the applicability of the common law rule of issue-estoppel.

law.fact: Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is the statutory embodiment of the rule of 'autrefois acquit' (double jeopardy).
law.text_evidence: Section 403, Criminal Procedure Code embodies in statutory form the accepted English rule of autrefois acquit.

law.fact: This section prevents a person who has been tried, and either convicted or acquitted, from being tried again for the same offence.
law.text_evidence: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence...

law.fact: The common law rule of 'issue-estoppel' prevents a specific issue of fact, which has been decided in favor of an accused in a previous trial, from being re-litigated in a subsequent trial between the same parties.
law.text_evidence: The question is whether where an issue of fact has been tried by a competent court on a former occasion and a finding has been reached in favour of an accused, such a finding would constitute an estoppel or res judicata against the prosecution, not as a bar to the trial and conviction of the accused for a different offence but as precluding the reception of evidence to disturb that finding of fact...

application.fact: The Court directly rejected the argument that Section 403 is exhaustive and therefore prevents the application of issue-estoppel.
application.text_evidence: Pritam Singh's case(') required reconsideration because the principle could have no application to India where the principle of autrefois acquit is covered by a statutory provision viz., s. 403, · B Criminal Procedure Code which must be taken to be exhaustive in character. We are unable to accept this contention as right.

application.fact: The Court distinguished between the two rules, clarifying that they operate differently. Section 403 bars a new trial for the same offence, whereas issue-estoppel bars the re-litigation of a specific factual finding in a trial for a different offence.
application.text_evidence: The rule of issue-estoppel is not covered by s. 403, Criminal Procedure Code, which deals with the principle of autrefois acquit : but that section does not preclude the applicability of the rule.

application.fact: The Court affirmed that issue-estoppel is a valid and sound legal principle, citing its own prior decisions in 'Pritam Singh' and 'Manipur Administration' that had already accepted the rule.
application.text_evidence: In any event, the rule is one which is in accordance with sound principle and supported by high authority and there are already two decisions of this Court, viz., Pritam Singh's case(') and a later case Manipur Administration v. Thokchom, Bira Singh(')-which have accepted the rule as a proper one to be adopted. We therefore do not see any reason for casting any doubt on the soundness of the rule...

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not exhaustive. It held that Section 403, which codifies the rule against double jeopardy ('autrefois acquit'), operates separately from the common law rule of issue-estoppel. While Section 403 prevents a re-trial for the same offence, issue-estoppel prevents the re-litigation of a specific factual issue already decided in an accused's favor. Therefore, the existence of the statutory provision in Section 403 does not preclude the application of the common law rule of issue-estoppel.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rule of issue-estoppel is applicable in criminal trials in India, distinct from the principle of autrefois acquit under Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that because a prior complaint involving the same facts was dismissed by a Magistrate, the subsequent prosecution and conviction for forgery must fail. This is based on the principle that an issue of fact, once decided in the accused's favor, cannot be re-litigated.
respondent_arguments: The respondent contended that the precedents establishing the rule of issue-estoppel in India, such as Pritam Singh's case, were based on foreign judgments and should not be applied.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is exhaustive in character and thereby precludes the applicability of the common law rule of issue-estoppel.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument for applying issue-estoppel inherently assumes that Section 403 is not exhaustive and that common law principles can operate alongside the statute.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position was that the prosecution was permissible under Section 403(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, implying that the statute is the complete and only law on the subject and that no other principle, like issue-estoppel, should be considered.

cases.case_name: Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Cited as a precedent that applied and accepted the rule of issue-estoppel as a proper one to be adopted in India.

cases.case_name: Manipur Administration v. Thockechom Bira Singh
cases.principle: Cited as a precedent that applied and accepted the rule of issue-estoppel as a proper one to be adopted in India.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The rule of issue-estoppel, which prevents the relitigation of an issue of fact that has been decided in a prior case by a competent court between the same parties, is applicable in criminal law and is not precluded by Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
obiter: The rule of issue-estoppel is in accordance with sound principle and is supported by high authority.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the earlier criminal case, the allegation that the executant's thumb impressions on blank forms were obtained by force, was found to be false. That finding was final and could not be reopened because of the rule as to issue-estoppel. Therefore, the sub-stratum of the present case failed and the appellants could not be convicted for the offence of forgery and its abetment.
legal_tests_applied: The rule of issue-estoppel, which questions whether where an issue of fact has been tried by a competent court on a former occasion and a finding has been reached in favour of an accused, such a finding would constitute an estoppel or res judicata against the prosecution, not as a bar to the trial and conviction of the accused for a different offence but as precluding the reception of evidence to disturb that finding of fact when the accused is tried subsequently even for a different offence which might be permitted by the terms of s. 403(2), Criminal Procedure Code.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's argument that Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code is exhaustive and precludes the rule of issue-estoppel was rejected. The court held: 'The rule of issue-estoppel is not covered by s. 403, Criminal Procedure Code, which deals with the principle of autrefois acquit : but that section does not preclude the applicability of the rule.'

The respondent's contention that prior Supreme Court decisions establishing issue-estoppel should be reconsidered because they were based on foreign judgments was rejected. The court affirmed that 'the rule is one which is in accordance with sound principle and supported by high authority' and saw 'no reason for casting any doubt on the soundness of the rule or for taking a different view from that adopted in the two earlier decisions of this Court referred to.'
why_respondent_won: The appellant's argument that the rule of issue-estoppel applies in India as a principle distinct from autrefois acquit under Section 403 was accepted. The court explicitly distinguished between the two, defining issue-estoppel as an 'objection to the reception of evidence to prove an identical fact which has been the subject-matter of an earlier finding between the same parties.'

The appellant's argument that the prior dismissal of a complaint based on the same facts barred the subsequent forgery conviction was accepted. The court applied the rule directly: 'If the rule of issue-estoppel is applied to the present case, it follows that the charge with regard to forgery must fail against all the appellants.' This was because the earlier finding that the thumb impressions were not obtained by force was 'final and could not be reopened.'
policy_considerations: The court endorsed the rule of issue-estoppel as being 'in accordance with sound principle and supported by high authority,' indicating a policy preference for judicial finality and consistency.

The principle of fairness, preventing the state from re-litigating a factual issue already decided in an accused's favor, is central. The court quoted with approval: 'Once that is done, then, so long as the finding stands, if there be any subsequent litigation between the same parties, no allegations legally inconsistent with the finding may be made by one of them against the other.'
